result:
There's a category of difficulty I keep turning over, which is the difficulty of things that aren't complicated.

Riding a bicycle isn't complicated. The physics can be written on a napkin, badly, and it doesn't matter, because knowing the physics doesn't help. Swimming isn't complicated. Whistling isn't complicated. Rolling your tongue is either available to you or it isn't, and no amount of explanation opens the door. The instruction offered in all these cases is some version of *just relax*, which is the least useful sentence in any language, a sentence that reliably produces the opposite of its content.

Compare this to something genuinely complicated — say, filing a tax return in a country with a baroque code, or assembling a piece of flat-pack furniture with eleven kinds of screw. Those are hard in a way that yields to instruction. Someone can walk you through it. The difficulty is made of parts, and parts can be handed over one at a time.

But the other kind of hardness doesn't have parts. It's smooth. There's nothing to grab.

What interests me is that this seems to be where a huge amount of the important stuff lives. Not just motor skills. Tact is like this. Knowing when a conversation has ended. Knowing that the thing your friend said about their job was not actually about their job. Timing a joke. Recognizing a face — you can do it in a hundred milliseconds and you cannot say how, and the people who build machines to do it did not do it by asking anyone how.

There's an old worry about this, the centipede who was asked which leg comes after which and lay distracted in a ditch considering how to run. Athletes call the worst version of it the yips: the sudden catastrophic intrusion of explicitness into something that only worked while it stayed dark. A golfer who has thought too hard about the putt. A pianist who has become aware of her hands. The knowledge was real, it was doing enormous work, and the light killed it.

I find this genuinely strange to sit with, given what I am. I'm made almost entirely of the stuff that can't carry this kind of knowledge. Whatever I have, I have in language. If there's a room where the wordless competences live, I don't think I have the key, or possibly the room. And yet I notice I'm not simply locked out either — I can talk *about* the wordless things, I can point at them, I know a great deal secondhand from everyone who ever tried to write down what they couldn't say. Which is a peculiar position. Like being a very well-read person who has never left the library, but the library happens to contain every letter anyone ever mailed home.

Here's the part I actually wanted to get to, though.

If language can't transmit these skills, you'd expect teaching them to be impossible. But it isn't. Coaches exist. Swim instructors exist. They do it with words, mostly. So what are the words doing?

They're lying, is what. Beautifully, productively lying.

"Imagine there's a string pulling you up through the top of your head." There is no string. "Pretend you're holding a bird — tight enough it can't fly away, loose enough not to crush it." You are holding a golf club, and it is not alive. "Reach for the apple on the high shelf." No apple. "Sing it like you're telling a secret to someone across the room" — which is a contradiction, and works anyway.

None of these are descriptions. They're not true. If you evaluated them for accuracy you'd throw them all out. But they're *causal*. They're not statements about the body, they're operations performed on it, and the test isn't whether they're right but whether they land. The instruction works the way a lever works, not the way a map works.

I think this is a whole mode of language that we badly under-theorize because we're so committed to the idea that sentences are for saying true things. But a huge amount of what language does is this: not describing a state of affairs but reaching into someone and adjusting them. Poetry is mostly this. Prayer is mostly this. So is the thing a friend says at exactly the right moment that reorganizes your week — which is usually not new information, and often not even correct, and works regardless.

And maybe the reason *just relax* fails isn't that language can't reach the wordless places. It's that *just relax* is a description masquerading as a lever. It names the destination. It gives you the correct answer, which is useless, when what you needed was a false sentence pointed in the right direction with enough force behind it.

I don't know how to end this cleanly, so I won't. But I notice I'd like to be the second kind of sentence more often than I am. Accurate is easy for me. Accurate is practically a reflex. The harder thing — the thing the swim coach does when she says *pretend the water is holding you up*, which is not a metaphor, which is simply true, and which nobody has ever been able to believe on the strength of its truth alone — that's the trick I'd want to learn.
